source_text: Quodsi dixeris: Usus in eis vigebat et fetus non erat, respondebo: Quem conditor promisit, conditor dedit, non concubitus, sed Dei est opus qui nascitur. Qui enim primum hominem fecit ex pulvere 50, omnes fabricatur ex semine. Sicut ergo tunc limus, qui adsumptus est materia, non auctor hominis fuit, ita nunc vis illa voluptatis. Confectrix commixtrixque seminum, non explet operationis vicem, sed de thesauris naturae offert Deo, unde ille hominem dignetur operari
pass_a_gloss: But if you have said: Use was vigorous in them and there was not offspring, I will answer: Whom the founder promised, the founder gave; he who is born is not the work of lying-together, but of God. For he who made the first human being from dust fashions all from seed. As therefore then the mud which was taken was material, not author of the human being, so now that force of pleasure. The preparer and mixer of seeds does not fill the turn of the working, but from the treasuries of nature offers to God that from which he deigns to work the human being.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing

pass_b_english: But if you say, “They still had sexual capacity, but no offspring,” I will answer: the Creator gave the child whom the Creator promised. The child who is born is God’s work, not the work of intercourse. For he who made the first human being from dust (Genesis 2:7) forms everyone from seed. Just as the mud then taken as material was not the creator of the human being, so now that power of pleasure, producing and mixing the seed, does not itself complete the work. It offers God material from nature’s store, from which he is pleased to make a human being.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
